headline: Auxly, MediPharm and MariMed grow Q3 revenue as margins diverge
dek: Auxly's sales rose 24% at a 32% EBITDA margin, MediPharm's German revenue jumped 81%, and MariMed hit record revenue while wholesale prices squeezed margins.
key_points: Auxly Cannabis Group grew third-quarter net revenue 24% to $49.5 million, with adjusted EBITDA up 29% to $15.8 million, a 32% margin.
MediPharm Labs' revenue rose 18% from the second quarter to $11.8 million, led by Germany, where sales rose 81% year on year, but its gross margin fell to 32% from 43%.
MariMed posted record revenue of $44.2 million, up 8.5%, but its GAAP net loss widened to $3.5 million as wholesale price compression cut margins.
By MetaFlora's calculation, adjusted EBITDA margins ranged from about 4% at MediPharm to 11% at MariMed and 32% at Auxly.
body: Three smaller listed cannabis companies reported third-quarter results on 11 and 12 November, and all three grew revenue. What separates them is how much of that growth reached the bottom line. Auxly Cannabis Group, a Canadian consumer products maker, turned a 24% sales increase into a 32% adjusted EBITDA margin. MediPharm Labs, a Canadian pharmaceutical-style extract producer, grew fastest in Germany but saw its gross margin fall sharply. MariMed, a US multistate operator, set a revenue record while wholesale price compression kept it loss-making.

The figures below are as each company reported them in its results release, in its own reporting currency. Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP measure each company defines differently, so the comparison is indicative rather than exact.
## Auxly: volume, pricing and a low cost base

Auxly said net revenue for the quarter to 30 September was $49.5 million, up 24% from $39.9 million a year earlier, driven by higher volumes across its core brands and better flower pricing, partly offset by price compression in vapes. Its gross margin on finished inventory held at 56%. Adjusted EBITDA rose 29% to $15.8 million.

Net income was $13.6 million, down from a year earlier, but the prior-year quarter included an $8.1 million after-tax gain on a debenture settlement with Imperial Brands. Excluding that gain and fair-value adjustments, Auxly said net income rose 70%. Selling, general and administrative costs fell to 27.7% of revenue from 29.2%.

The balance sheet is in good shape for a Canadian producer. Auxly ended the quarter with $51.4 million in cash against $43.4 million of debt, which by MetaFlora's arithmetic leaves it about $8 million net cash positive, and debt of 0.8 times trailing adjusted EBITDA. It bought back 2.7 million shares for $6.1 million in the first nine months and plans up to $30 million of capital spending through 2028 to lift capacity at its Auxly Leamington facility by 30% from 2025 levels. It said it is evaluating export opportunities, with a measured approach.

MediPharm Labs reported revenue of $11.8 million, up 18% from the second quarter, with net income of $112,000, its second profitable quarter in a row, and adjusted EBITDA of $442,000. International medical sales were $6.9 million, or 59% of the total. German revenue rose 19% from the second quarter and 81% from a year earlier, across flower, oil and dronabinol, and sales in other international markets, including the UK and Brazil, rose to $1.8 million from $0.7 million.

The cost of that growth shows in the margin. MediPharm's own quarterly table shows gross margin of 32% in the third quarter, down from 43% in the second and 37% in the first, though still above 26% a year earlier. Operating expenses fell 11% from the second quarter to about $3.6 million, which kept the company in profit. At home, Canadian medical revenue was flat at $2.3 million, held back by Veterans Affairs Canada's 30% cut in its maximum reimbursement rate, from $8.50 to $6.00 a gram, from 1 April.

MediPharm ended the quarter with $10.1 million in cash and described itself as virtually debt free. After the quarter, it made its first commercial shipment of CBD metered-dose inhalers to Panama; as we reported on 9 November, the inhaler has also received a notified-body opinion that supports a route to the UK and EU markets.
> Growth is no longer the hard part for these companies. Keeping margin while selling into falling prices is.

MariMed's revenue reached $44.2 million, its highest ever, up 5.5% from the second quarter and 8.5% from a year earlier. For the first nine months, revenue was $125.6 million, up about 6% from $118.2 million. Wholesale revenue rose 8.1% year on year and retail 8.4%, with transactions across its Thrive dispensaries up 7% and its branded products sold into 721 stores.

Profitability moved the other way. MariMed's non-GAAP gross margin was 40%, about 140 basis points lower than a year earlier, which it attributed to continued wholesale price compression. Adjusted EBITDA was $4.7 million, up 18% from the second quarter but down from $5.1 million a year earlier, and the GAAP net loss widened to $3.5 million from $2.9 million. Cash rose to $10.4 million, its strongest position in two years. Chief executive Jon Levine named the timing of Section 280E tax relief and banking reform as potential catalysts.

Adjusted EBITDA as a share of revenue was about 32% at Auxly, 11% at MariMed and under 4% at MediPharm, by MetaFlora's calculation from the reported figures. Auxly's margin reflects a large, mature Canadian brand business running on a fixed cost base. MariMed's reflects the US wholesale squeeze that other operators have also reported this earnings season. MediPharm is the smallest, and its profit depends on keeping costs down while it shifts towards international medical sales, where Germany's market is under political pressure over telemedicine and reimbursement.

For Auxly, watch whether it commits to exports and how quickly the Leamington expansion adds capacity. For MediPharm, the key signals are whether gross margin recovers from 32% and whether German demand holds as Berlin weighs prescription restrictions. For MariMed, the next markers are the fourth-quarter wholesale price trend and any federal tax relief, which would change the economics of its Massachusetts, Maryland, Illinois and Delaware operations.
